name: THE MAMA TOLD ME GNOCCHI COME

recipe.history:
Gnocchi — the small, pillowy Italian dumplings most commonly made from potato — have a culinary history that predates the potato entirely. Before the Columbian Exchange brought the potato to Europe in the sixteenth century, Italian gnocchi were made from semolina, bread, and other starchy ingredients, and their name derives from the Italian word for a knot of wood, describing the small, dense shape. Potato gnocchi as we know them today became prevalent in Northern Italy — particularly in Veneto, Friuli, and Trentino — during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, after the potato had been fully adopted into the Italian agricultural diet. The technique of ricing cooked potato and combining it with just enough flour to bind — the essential discipline of gnocchi-making — is one of the great exercises in culinary restraint: too much flour and the gnocchi are dense and leaden, too little and they fall apart in the water. The perfect gnocchi is light, yielding, and almost melts in the mouth, and pan-frying in brown butter — the classical Italian preparation — gives the exterior a golden, slightly crispy shell that contrasts beautifully with the soft interior.

Brown butter — beurre noisette in French, burro nocciola in Italian — is made by cooking butter past its melting point until the milk solids caramelize and the fat itself takes on the color and aroma of toasted hazelnuts. It is one of the simplest and most transformative techniques in European cookery, appearing in both French and Italian culinary traditions as a finishing element for pasta, gnocchi, fish, and vegetables. Fried sage leaves in brown butter — the classic accompaniment to pan-fried gnocchi — add a herbal, slightly camphor-like note that cuts through the butter's richness and perfumes the whole dish. As a burger topping, pan-fried gnocchi in brown butter and sage is an act of deliberate extravagance: carbohydrate on carbohydrate, fat on fat, the gnocchi acting as a textural surprise that transforms the burger from a simple sandwich into something that feels vaguely like an Italian-American dinner in the compressed format of a handheld meal.

My mother made gnocchi from scratch exactly once a year, on the Sunday closest to my grandmother's birthday, using a recipe she claimed came from my great-grandmother who had emigrated from Emilia-Romagna. I was allowed to help rice the potatoes, which I considered an honor because it meant I got to operate the ricer, which I found unreasonably satisfying. The gnocchi were always served with brown butter and fried sage, because that was how the recipe specified them, and my mother held to recipes with a fundamentalism that I have always respected even when I have not inherited it. The first time I pan-fried leftover gnocchi the next morning and put them on a burger as an experiment, I felt simultaneously creative and slightly criminal, as if I were violating something. The result was too good to feel guilty about for long.

Pan-fried gnocchi on a burger creates a specific and demanding set of requirements. The gnocchi must be crispy on the outside and yielding within; the brown butter must be nutty and warm; the sage must be crisp. All of these things are perishable — they are best for approximately five minutes after they come out of the pan. This means the patty must also be ready at the same time, which means the cook must orchestrate the timing correctly, which means the patty must be pulled at exactly medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — not a degree more, so that the carry-over heat during its resting period does not push it into medium. The gnocchi wait for no one, and neither does the window of medium rare. This burger is a lesson in timing, in attention, and in the belief that the only correct temperature for a beef patty is the one that produces the most beautiful result.
ingredients: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
150g to 200g all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
fine sea salt and black pepper
170g aged provolone or fontina, sliced (for melting on the patty)
fine sea salt and white pepper
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Roast the garlic for the aioli: Preheat oven to 400°F (200°C). Cut the top off the garlic head to expose the cloves. Drizzle with olive oil, wrap in foil, and roast for 40 to 45 minutes until completely soft and caramelized. Squeeze out the roasted cloves, mash into a paste, and combine with mayonnaise, lemon juice, salt, and white pepper. Refrigerate.

2. Make the buns (reduce oven to 375°F / 190°C after garlic): Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the stand mixer bowl with dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix, then add butter gradually. Knead on medium-high until smooth, 8 minutes. Rise until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours. Divide into 6 portions, shape, proof 40 minutes. Egg wash, sesame seeds, bake 18 to 20 minutes. Cool.

3. Make the gnocchi: Bake the russet potatoes whole at 400°F (200°C) until completely tender throughout, about 1 hour. (Baking rather than boiling keeps them dry, which is essential for light gnocchi.) While still hot, cut in half, scoop out the flesh, and pass through a ricer onto a clean work surface. Spread out and allow the steam to escape for 5 minutes.

4. Make a well in the center of the riced potato. Add 150g flour, the egg yolk, salt, and nutmeg. Mix gently with your hands until a dough just comes together. Add additional flour only if the dough is too sticky to handle — use as little flour as possible. Overworking or over-flouring makes dense gnocchi.

5. Divide the gnocchi dough into portions. On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion into a rope about 3/4 inch thick. Cut into 1-inch pieces. Roll each piece over the tines of a fork to create ridges that will hold the brown butter. Place on a floured baking sheet. (Gnocchi can be refrigerated on the baking sheet for up to 2 hours at this point.)

6. Cook the gnocchi in boiling salted water in batches: drop them in and cook until they float to the surface, about 2 to 3 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon to an oiled baking sheet to dry slightly.

7. Pan-fry the gnocchi: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add olive oil and 30g of butter. When the butter foams, add gnocchi in a single layer (work in batches). Do not stir for 2 minutes, allowing the bottoms to become golden and crispy. Flip and crisp the other side, 1 to 2 more minutes. In the last 30 seconds, add the remaining 60g butter and the sage leaves. Swirl the pan as the butter foams and turns golden-brown and nutty — beurre noisette. The sage leaves will crisp up in the brown butter. Season with salt and pepper. Remove from heat immediately.

8. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season generously with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

9. Cook the patties: Coordinate the timing so the gnocchi and patties finish simultaneously. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and lay provolone or fontina slices on each patty. Cook 2 to 2.5 more minutes. Add a splash of water and cover to steam-melt the cheese for 30 seconds. The internal temperature must reach 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — medium rare, the only correct temperature. Rest patties on a rack for 3 minutes.
10. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.

11. Assemble: Spread roasted garlic aioli on both bun halves. Layer baby spinach or arugula on the bottom bun, followed by a tomato slice. Place the cheese-covered patty on top. Immediately spoon a generous pile of pan-fried gnocchi in brown butter over the patty. Scatter the fried sage leaves on top. Finish with a generous grating of Parmigiano-Reggiano. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately — the gnocchi are at their best right now.
